[Chapter 12 · Large Language Models]{.eyebrow}

# Capstone — Build a GPT

[Assemble Chapter 11's transformer blocks into a character-level language model and train it by next-token prediction, the maximum likelihood of Chapter 2 at scale.]{.dek}
:::

The book ends where it has been heading since the first regression line. A [GPT]{.term} is a stack of the transformer blocks of Chapter 11, trained on one objective: predict the next token. That objective is [maximum likelihood]{.term}, the principle that produced ordinary least squares in Chapter 2, now applied to a categorical distribution over a vocabulary, exactly as in the softmax regression of Chapter 4. The capstone writes each piece you have read about, an attention head, a transformer block, the training loop, and autoregressive generation, then trains a model of about a third of a million parameters until it produces rough Shakespeare on a laptop.

The step-by-step structure follows Andrej Karpathy's *"Let's build GPT"* lecture and his [nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT); the code is our own, in the book's notation. For real tokenization and GPT-2-scale weights, nanoGPT is where to go next.

## Characters in, characters out

Production models tokenize text into sub-word pieces (Chapter 12). Here we keep things as simple as possible and work [character by character]{.term}, so the vocabulary is just the set of distinct characters in the corpus, Karpathy's *Tiny Shakespeare*, about a megabyte of the plays. An `encode` map sends each character to an integer and `decode` sends it back. A batch is a stack of random fixed-length windows, with the targets shifted one position right: at every position the model is asked to predict the next character. That one-position shift is the entire supervision signal. The model never sees a label beyond "what came next."

## The same idea, with a context of one

The capstone needs PyTorch and so runs in Colab. The idea it scales up needs nothing but numpy, and it runs here. A [bigram model]{.term} predicts the next character from the current one and nothing else: count how often each character follows each other character, then normalize each row of counts into a probability vector. That normalization *is* the maximum likelihood estimate of a categorical distribution, the estimator behind Chapter 4's softmax regression in its simplest form, and the row it hands back is sampled exactly as the GPT's softmax output is, one character at a time.

This is not a metaphor for a language model. It is a language model, fitted by the same principle and generating by the same procedure. The structural difference is the length of the context: the capstone conditions on sixty-four characters and learns, through attention, what to make of them; the bigram conditions on one and holds nothing but a table of counts.

The text below is a passage of *Coriolanus* from the capstone's own corpus, written inline so the cell stands on its own. Letters are lowercased and everything else becomes a space, leaving 1,041 characters over a vocabulary of 27. One detail deserves the attention it gets in the code: a character the passage never uses — here `x` — has an empty row of counts, and normalizing it would divide by zero. Such rows get the uniform distribution instead, and an assertion checks that every row sums to one before anything is sampled.

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

## Python
```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# A passage of Coriolanus (Tiny Shakespeare, the capstone's corpus), inline so
# the cell stands alone and Python and R count exactly the same text.
TEXT = """MENENIUS:
Do not stand upon't.
We recommend to you, tribunes of the people,
Our purpose to them: and to our noble consul
Wish we all joy and honour.

Senators:
To Coriolanus come all joy and honour!

BRUTUS:
You see how he intends to use the people.

SICINIUS:
May they perceive's intent! He will require them,
As if he did contemn what he requested
Should be in them to give.

BRUTUS:
Come, we'll inform them
Of our proceedings here: on the marketplace,
I know, they do attend us.

First Citizen:
Once, if he do require our voices, we ought not to deny him.

Second Citizen:
We may, sir, if we will.

Third Citizen:
We have power in ourselves to do it, but it is a
power that we have no power to do; for if he show us
his wounds and tell us his deeds, we are to put our
tongues into those wounds and speak for them; so, if
he tell us his noble deeds, we must also tell him
our noble acceptance of them. Ingratitude is
monstrous, and for the multitude to be ingrateful,
were to make a monster of the multitude: of the
which we being members, should bring ourselves to be
monstrous members."""

# Vocabulary: 26 letters and a space. Everything else becomes a space.
alphabet = " abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
K = len(alphabet)
pos = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(alphabet)}
clean = " ".join("".join(c if c in pos else " " for c in TEXT.lower()).split())
print(f"{len(clean)} characters, vocabulary of {K}")

# Count every adjacent pair: counts[i, j] = times j followed i
counts = np.zeros((K, K))
for a, b in zip(clean, clean[1:]):
    counts[pos[a], pos[b]] += 1

# Maximum likelihood: each row of counts, normalized. A character the passage
# never uses has an empty row, so give it the uniform rather than divide by zero.
row_total = counts.sum(axis=1)
empty = row_total == 0
P = counts / np.where(empty, 1.0, row_total)[:, None]   # 1.0 dodges the 0/0
P[empty] = 1.0 / K                                      # unseen context: uniform
assert np.allclose(P.sum(axis=1), 1.0), "every row must be a probability vector"
print("contexts never seen (given the uniform):", [alphabet[i] for i in np.flatnonzero(empty)])

# What the counts say about a few contexts. Only successors the passage actually
# supplies: a zero-probability "top" entry is an artifact of sorting, not a fact.
for c in "qth":
    ranked = np.argsort(-P[pos[c]])[:3]
    top = [j for j in ranked if P[pos[c], j] > 0]
    print(f"  after '{c}':  " + "   ".join(
        f"'{alphabet[j]}' {P[pos[c], j]:.2f}" for j in top))

# In-sample cross-entropy: the average -log p the model assigns its own text
p_seen = np.array([P[pos[a], pos[b]] for a, b in zip(clean, clean[1:])])
ce = -np.log(p_seen).mean()
print(f"in-sample cross-entropy {ce:.3f} nats  (perplexity {np.exp(ce):.2f})")

# Sample from the model: one character conditioned on the last, 240 times
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
prev, out = " ", []
for _ in range(240):
    prev = alphabet[rng.choice(K, p=P[pos[prev]])]
    out.append(prev)
print("\nsampled:", "".join(out))

# Transition probabilities over a readable slice of the alphabet
show = " aehinoqrstu"
idx = [pos[c] for c in show]
labels = ["·" if c == " " else c for c in show]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
im = ax.imshow(P[np.ix_(idx, idx)], cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.03, label="P(next | current)")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(show)))
ax.set_xticklabels(labels)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(show)))
ax.set_yticklabels(labels)
ax.tick_params(colors="#666666")
ax.set_xlabel("next character")
ax.set_ylabel("current character")
ax.set_title("Bigram transition probabilities")
for s in ax.spines.values():
    s.set_color("#cfccc2")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## R
```{webr}
# A passage of Coriolanus (Tiny Shakespeare, the capstone's corpus), inline so
# the cell stands alone and Python and R count exactly the same text.
TEXT <- "MENENIUS:
Do not stand upon't.
We recommend to you, tribunes of the people,
Our purpose to them: and to our noble consul
Wish we all joy and honour.

Senators:
To Coriolanus come all joy and honour!

BRUTUS:
You see how he intends to use the people.

SICINIUS:
May they perceive's intent! He will require them,
As if he did contemn what he requested
Should be in them to give.

BRUTUS:
Come, we'll inform them
Of our proceedings here: on the marketplace,
I know, they do attend us.

First Citizen:
Once, if he do require our voices, we ought not to deny him.

Second Citizen:
We may, sir, if we will.

Third Citizen:
We have power in ourselves to do it, but it is a
power that we have no power to do; for if he show us
his wounds and tell us his deeds, we are to put our
tongues into those wounds and speak for them; so, if
he tell us his noble deeds, we must also tell him
our noble acceptance of them. Ingratitude is
monstrous, and for the multitude to be ingrateful,
were to make a monster of the multitude: of the
which we being members, should bring ourselves to be
monstrous members."

# Vocabulary: 26 letters and a space. Everything else becomes a space.
alphabet <- c(" ", letters)
K <- length(alphabet)
ch <- strsplit(tolower(TEXT), "")[[1]]
ch[!(ch %in% alphabet)] <- " "
clean <- strsplit(trimws(gsub(" +", " ", paste(ch, collapse = ""))), "")[[1]]
cat(sprintf("%d characters, vocabulary of %d\n", length(clean), K))

# Count every adjacent pair: counts[i, j] = times j followed i
i <- match(clean, alphabet)
counts <- matrix(0, K, K)
for (t in seq_len(length(i) - 1)) counts[i[t], i[t + 1]] <- counts[i[t], i[t + 1]] + 1

# Maximum likelihood: each row of counts, normalized. A character the passage
# never uses has an empty row, so give it the uniform rather than divide by zero.
row_total <- rowSums(counts)
P <- counts / ifelse(row_total > 0, row_total, 1)
P[row_total == 0, ] <- 1 / K
stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(P) - 1) < 1e-12))
cat("contexts never seen (given the uniform):",
    paste(alphabet[row_total == 0], collapse = " "), "\n")

# What the counts say about a few contexts. Only successors the passage actually
# supplies: a zero-probability "top" entry is an artifact of sorting, not a fact.
for (c in c("q", "t", "h")) {
  r <- match(c, alphabet)
  ranked <- order(P[r, ], decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
  top <- ranked[P[r, ranked] > 0]
  cat(sprintf("  after '%s': ", c),
      paste(sprintf("'%s' %.2f", alphabet[top], P[r, top]), collapse = "   "), "\n")
}

# In-sample cross-entropy: the average -log p the model assigns its own text
p_seen <- P[cbind(i[-length(i)], i[-1])]
cat(sprintf("in-sample cross-entropy %.3f nats  (perplexity %.2f)\n",
            mean(-log(p_seen)), exp(mean(-log(p_seen)))))

# Sample from the model: one character conditioned on the last, 240 times
set.seed(0)
prev <- 1
out <- character(240)
for (t in seq_len(240)) {
  prev <- sample(K, 1, prob = P[prev, ])
  out[t] <- alphabet[prev]
}
cat("\nsampled:", paste(out, collapse = ""), "\n")

# Transition probabilities over a readable slice of the alphabet
show <- c(" ", "a", "e", "h", "i", "n", "o", "q", "r", "s", "t", "u")
idx <- match(show, alphabet)
labs <- ifelse(show == " ", "·", show)
M <- P[idx, idx]
n <- length(idx)

blues <- colorRampPalette(c("#f7fbff", "#deebf7", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1",
                            "#6baed6", "#4292c6", "#2171b5", "#08519c", "#08306b"))
image(1:n, 1:n, t(M[n:1, ]), col = blues(100), zlim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE,
      xlab = "next character", ylab = "current character",
      main = "Bigram transition probabilities")
axis(1, at = 1:n, labels = labs, col = "#cfccc2", col.axis = "#666666")
axis(2, at = n:1, labels = labs, las = 1, col = "#cfccc2", col.axis = "#666666")
box(col = "#cfccc2")
```

:::

The table recovers things that look like knowledge. All three `q`s in the passage sit inside *require* or *requested*, so the estimate of P(`u` | `q`) is 1.00 — a real regularity of English, learned from three observations and asserted with a confidence those three observations do not warrant. Unsmoothed maximum likelihood does this whenever counts are sparse, which is why the darkest cell in the heatmap is also the one resting on the least evidence; a shrunk estimate, Chapter 7's regularization in its categorical form, would pull it back off 1. Elsewhere the counts are better supported: `h` is followed by `e` in 0.51 of its cases, and `t` by `h` in 0.23 of the 74 times `t` occurs.

Sampling from the table gives text with the texture of English and none of its structure. The Python cell prints, from seed 0:

> `s a trengus t t the acose yotothathecoweingher r to ud d te l bl s we rs we ruthings tow`

Short common words survive — `the`, `to`, `we`, and later in the same sample `she` and `then` — because their letters follow one another often enough to be reassembled by luck. Nothing longer does, because the model discards each character the moment it has written the next. The R cell computes the same counts and the same probabilities, but draws from a different random generator, so its sampled text reads differently; only the numbers are expected to match.

The cross-entropy the cell reports, 2.013 nats, is not a number to set beside the figure at the top of this page. It is measured on the very text that produced the counts, over an alphabet of 27 rather than 65, and it rewards the model for memorizing a thousand characters rather than for predicting anything it has not seen. Held-out evaluation (Chapter 6) is what makes such a number mean something, and it is the held-out curve that the capstone reports.

What the capstone adds to this is memory. Attention lets the character at position *t* weigh every character before it, with weights that are learned rather than counted, so a prediction can depend on how a line began sixty characters earlier and not only on the character just written. That is the machinery the rest of this page builds.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}

Extend the count table from bigrams to trigrams: index the counts by the previous *two* characters and renormalize. The context grows from 27 rows to 729, the same 1,041 characters must now support 27 times as many parameters, and many more rows come back empty. Watch what that does to the sampled text, and to how often the uniform fallback fires — it is the data-hungriness of Chapter 12's scaling laws, arriving early.
:::

## A transformer block

The heart of a block is [self-attention]{.term} (Chapter 11). Each position is projected to a query, a key, and a value; every query is scored against every key; the scores are scaled by the square root of the head width to keep the softmax out of saturation; a [causal mask]{.term} forces position *t* to ignore everything after it; and a softmax turns the surviving scores into weights that mix the values. [Multi-head attention]{.term} runs several such heads in parallel slices of the model width and concatenates them. A block follows that with a position-wise feed-forward network, and wraps each sublayer in the two devices that make deep transformers trainable: a [residual connection]{.term}, the gradient highway of Chapter 9, and [layer normalization]{.term} applied before each sublayer.

PyTorch wants a numerical stack and ideally a GPU, more than a browser sandbox can carry, and the notebook downloads a small text corpus to train on, so the capstone runs in Google Colab: one click, free hardware, no local install.

```{=html}
<a class="colab-btn" href="https://colab.research.google.com/github/welr/learning_machines/blob/main/ch12_01_build_a_gpt.ipynb" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><span class="dot"></span> Open the capstone in Google Colab</a>
```

The code below is here for reference; open it in Colab to run and modify it. A block is attention then feed-forward, each computed on a normalized copy of the input and added back through the residual.

```python
import torch.nn as nn

class Block(nn.Module):
    """A transformer block: pre-norm attention and feed-forward, each with a residual."""
    def __init__(self, n_embd, n_head):
        super().__init__()
        head_size = n_embd // n_head
        self.attn = MultiHeadAttention(n_head, head_size)
        self.ffwd = FeedForward()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))     # residual around attention
        x = x + self.ffwd(self.norm2(x))     # residual around feed-forward
        return x
```

## Next-token prediction is maximum likelihood

The full model strings it together: a token embedding and a position embedding (attention has no built-in sense of order), a stack of blocks, a final layer norm, and a linear head that maps each position to a score over the vocabulary. Given targets, `forward` returns the [cross-entropy]{.term} between those scores and the next characters. This is the next-token objective in full, and it is the same loss as Chapter 4's softmax regression, now evaluated at every position of every sequence.

::: {.defbox}
[The Next-Token Objective]{.lbl}

[ minimize &nbsp; &minus;&sum;<sub>t</sub> log p<sub>&theta;</sub>(x<sub>t+1</sub> &nbsp;|&nbsp; x<sub>1</sub>,&hellip;,x<sub>t</sub>) &nbsp;=&nbsp; cross-entropy &nbsp;=&nbsp; the MLE of Chapter 2 ]{.math}
:::

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

class GPTLanguageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Block(n_embd, n_head) for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.norm_final = nn.LayerNorm(n_embd)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok = self.token_embedding(idx)                              # (B, T, n_embd)
        pos = self.position_embedding(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_final(self.blocks(tok + pos))
        logits = self.lm_head(x)                                     # (B, T, vocab_size)
        if targets is None:
            return logits, None
        # next-token cross-entropy: the maximum likelihood of Chapter 2, at scale
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(B * T, vocab_size), targets.view(B * T))
        return logits, loss
```

## Training

Minimizing that average cross-entropy is the training loop you already met in Chapter 9 and used unchanged in Chapter 10. Draw a batch, compute the loss, zero the gradients, backpropagate, step the optimizer. Only the model and the data differ. Alongside the loss it is worth reporting the [perplexity]{.term}, the exponential of the cross-entropy, the effective number of equally likely characters the model is choosing among at each step.

```python
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)

for step in range(max_iters + 1):
    x, y = get_batch("train")             # windows of characters; y is x shifted one right
    _, loss = model(x, y)                 # forward pass returns the next-token cross-entropy
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()                       # backpropagation
    optimizer.step()                      # theta <- theta - lr * grad
```

To generate, the model runs forward one character at a time: take the logits at the last position, turn them into a distribution, sample, append, and repeat. This is [autoregressive decoding]{.term}. Two controls from Chapter 12 shape the output: a [temperature]{.term} that divides the logits before the softmax, sharpening or flattening the distribution, and an optional [top-k]{.term} truncation that keeps only the most probable characters.

A third of a million parameters, trained for a couple of minutes on a megabyte of text, learns the *shape* of the data: line breaks, speaker labels in capitals, the rhythm of the verse, plausible-looking words. It is not yet coherent. That gap is the subject of Chapter 12's scaling laws, in which the cross-entropy floor lies far below where we are and the way down is more parameters and more data, grown together. nanoGPT is this same architecture scaled up until the babble becomes fluent.

::: {.explore}
[Try it]{.lbl}

In Colab, train for a few hundred steps and watch the loss fall, then sample at temperatures 0.5, 0.8, and 1.2 and compare. Low temperature is cautious and repetitive; high temperature is adventurous and error-prone. Then swap *Tiny Shakespeare* for a different corpus, a public-domain economics text, say, and re-run from the data step: the same estimator of Chapter 4 learns an entirely different voice.
:::
